title: Agoda vs Booking.com hotel prices: compare them with Python
summary:
"Is Agoda cheaper than Booking.com?" has no general answer, but it has a precise one for a given city and stay, and it takes about sixty lines of Python. This tutorial runs the same search on both sites, Rome, three nights a month from now, two adults, prices in euros, then does the part that usually goes wrong: recognising the same hotel on two sites that name it differently. The result is a table of matched hotels with an all-in price per night on each site, the gap in percent, and a count of which site wins. The data comes from two Apify Actors with the same output columns, the Agoda Hotels Scraper and the Booking.com Hotels Scraper, called through the official Python client.

What you need

  • An Apify account (the free plan is enough to try this) and its API token, from Apify Console → Settings → API & Integrations, exported as an environment variable: export APIFY_TOKEN=...
  • Python 3 and two packages: 
pip install "apify-client>=3,<4" pandas

Step 1: the same stay on both sites

Both Actors take the stay the same way: checkInDaysFromNow and nights for a stay relative to today (so the script works the day you read it), or checkIn and checkOut for fixed dates. Save this as agoda_vs_booking.py:

import os

import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

stay = {"checkInDaysFromNow": 30, "nights": 3, "adults": 2, "currency": "EUR"}

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
booking_run = client.actor("myth84/booking-hotels-scraper").call(run_input={
    "location": "Rome, Italy", "destId": -126693, "propertyTypes": ["hotels"], "maxResults": 100, **stay,
})
agoda_run = client.actor("myth84/agoda-hotels-scraper").call(run_input={
    "location": "Rome", "sortBy": "RANKING", "maxResults": 150, **stay,
})
booking = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(booking_run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())
agoda = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(agoda_run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())

booking = booking[booking["priceTotal"].notna()].copy()
booking["allInPerNight"] = (booking["priceTotal"] + booking["taxesAndFees"].fillna(0)) / booking["nights"]
agoda = agoda[agoda["priceTotal"].notna()].copy()
agoda["allInPerNight"] = agoda["priceTotal"] / agoda["nights"]
print(len(booking), "priced hotels on Booking.com,", len(agoda), "on Agoda")

The inputs come from public tasks: "Cheapest stays in Rome next month" on Booking.com (its destId, the dest_id of a Booking.com search URL for Rome) and "Hotels in Rome under the best guest scores" on Agoda. The orders changed on purpose. Booking.com keeps hotels only (propertyTypes) in its default top-picks order instead of the cheapest first, and Agoda uses its own ranking (RANKING, which varies a little between requests) instead of the best scores first: comparing the cheapest properties of one site with the best-rated of the other would match almost nothing. Agoda gets more rows because it lists many more properties per city; more rows on either side raise the number of matches.

The all-in price per night is the line to compare, and the two sites build it differently:

  • Booking.com: priceTotal is the total of the stay before the charges Booking.com lists as excluded (city tax, VAT, service charges), which are in taxesAndFees. The all-in total is the sum of both.
  • Agoda: with the default priceView (inclusive), priceTotal already includes taxes and fees; taxesAndFees gives their amount.

Properties without a price for the stay (sold out, for instance) are set aside.

Step 2: recognise the same hotel

The two sites have their own ids, so platformListingId does not join them, and names vary: the same place can be "Hotel X Roma" on one side and "X Hotel" on the other, with accents or not. Two clues together are reliable: a similar name once the noise words are removed, and a position within a couple of hundred metres. Both Actors return latitude and longitude. Add this to the script:

import math
import re
import unicodedata
from difflib import SequenceMatcher

NOISE = {"hotel", "hotels", "rome", "roma", "the", "and", "by", "di", "de", "del", "la", "il"}


def name_key(title):
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", title).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode().lower()
    return " ".join(word for word in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text) if word not in NOISE)


def metres(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    x = math.radians(lon2 - lon1) * math.cos(math.radians((lat1 + lat2) / 2))
    return 6_371_000 * math.hypot(x, math.radians(lat2 - lat1))


booking = booking.dropna(subset=["latitude", "longitude"])
agoda = agoda.dropna(subset=["latitude", "longitude"])
booking["nameKey"] = booking["title"].map(name_key)
agoda["nameKey"] = agoda["title"].map(name_key)

matches = []
for b in booking.itertuples():
    best, best_score = None, 0.0
    for a in agoda.itertuples():
        if metres(b.latitude, b.longitude, a.latitude, a.longitude) > 250:
            continue
        score = 1.0 if a.nameKey == b.nameKey else SequenceMatcher(None, a.nameKey, b.nameKey).ratio()
        if score > best_score:
            best, best_score = a, score
    if best is not None and best_score >= 0.8:
        matches.append({
            "hotel": b.title, "agodaName": best.title, "stars": b.starRating, "nameScore": round(best_score, 2),
            "booking": round(b.allInPerNight, 2), "agoda": round(best.allInPerNight, 2),
        })

name_key removes accents, punctuation and the words every hotel in the city shares, then compares what is left. SequenceMatcher gives a similarity between 0 and 1; 0.8 within 250 metres keeps the obvious pairs and the small spelling differences. The distance test does most of the work for chains: two hotels of the same brand three kilometres apart never match. The agodaName and nameScore columns are there so you can check the pairs by eye; sort by nameScore and read the lowest ones first.

Step 3: which site is cheaper? 

table = pd.DataFrame(matches)
table["gapPercent"] = (100 * (table.agoda - table.booking) / table.booking).round(1)
table["cheaper"] = "same (within 1 %)"
table.loc[table["gapPercent"] < -1, "cheaper"] = "agoda"
table.loc[table["gapPercent"] > 1, "cheaper"] = "booking"

print(f"{len(table)} hotels found on both sites")
print(table["cheaper"].value_counts())
print("Median gap by stars (negative: Agoda cheaper):")
print(table.groupby("stars")["gapPercent"].median())
print(table.sort_values("gapPercent").head(10))
table.to_csv("rome-agoda-vs-booking.csv", index=False)

gapPercent is Agoda's all-in price per night compared with Booking.com's for the same hotel: −8 means Agoda is 8 % cheaper, +5 that Booking.com is. Differences under 1 % are counted as a tie, which is mostly rounding. The table by stars answers a narrower question that is often more useful: one site can be cheaper for budget hotels and the other for 4- and 5-star ones. The CSV keeps every pair with both names, for a spreadsheet or a second look.

Honest limits of the comparison

  • The match is partial. Each site returns its own selection in its own order, so only part of the hotels appear on both sides; how many depends on the city and on maxResults. A median over a few dozen matched hotels is a reasonable signal, not a market study.
  • Matching makes mistakes. A renamed hotel, or two hotels sharing a building, can be missed or paired wrongly. Raise the threshold to 0.9 for fewer false pairs, lower it for more pairs, and check the lowest nameScore rows.
  • Taxes are counted by each site. A local tax paid at the hotel, such as a city tax, can be in one site's figure and not the other's. Compare taxesAndFees on both sides before concluding that one site is cheaper.
  • One price per property: the cheapest offer of the search card for two adults in one room, not the same room type or the same cancellation terms on both sites.
  • Visitor prices, without an account or member discounts, in the chosen currency.
  • No personal data. Property facts, average scores and review counts; nothing about guests or reviewers.

Without code, and more cities

Each input is also a public task in Apify Console. Open "Hotels in Rome under the best guest scores" (Agoda) and "Cheapest stays in Rome next month" (Booking.com), align the stay, save both as your own tasks and schedule them at the same hour; the Output tabs export CSV with the same column names. For several cities, both Actors take a locations list with the same stay for every destination (["Paris", "Rome", "Barcelona"] on Agoda, ["Paris, France", "Rome, Italy", "Barcelona, Spain"] on Booking.com, as in the public tasks "Compare hotel prices in Paris, Rome and Barcelona"); run the matching per searchLocation.

Pricing is pay-per-event on both Actors, a fixed price per property saved: $2.00 per 1,000 on Agoda and $2.50 per 1,000 on Booking.com on Apify's Free plan, down to $1.29 and $1.69 on the higher plans. This comparison of 150 + 100 properties costs about $0.55. Use the data for analysis, respect the platforms' terms and local law, and do not republish listings.

title: How to Turn Audio into Text on a Computer
summary:
Sometimes you need to turn an existing recording into text: a voice memo, a voice message or a recorded conversation. This is called audio transcription. Below is how to turn audio into text on your computer — and which way is simpler.

What people usually transcribe

  • Voice messages and dictaphone notes.

  • Recordings of meetings and calls.

  • Interviews and lectures.

  • Audio from a video, when the words are what matter.

Way 1. Online services

There are websites where you upload an audio file and get text back. Handy for a single recording, but keep in mind: you are sending the audio to someone else's server. For personal or work conversations that is not always a good idea, and long files are often transcribed only for a fee.

Way 2. Speak it again on your computer

If there is no recording yet and you just need the text, it is sometimes easier to speak it again. The VoiceNote program is made for exactly that: press “Record”, say what you need, and the app types your speech as text for you. You can copy or save the finished text, and everything runs on your own computer, with nothing sent outside.

More about the VoiceNote program

How to improve transcription accuracy

  • The cleaner the recording, the better the result — less noise and echo.

  • Speech without a strong accent and without several overlapping voices is recognised more accurately.

  • Still reread the finished text and fix the punctuation.

FAQ

Can I transcribe a long recording all at once?**Yes, but long files are easier to handle in parts — it is simpler to check and edit the text.

Will my conversation go to someone else's server?****If that matters, choose a tool that runs on your own computer. VoiceNote sends nothing outside.

Which language does recognition work in?**
Russian and other languages.

In short

  • A one-off, non-personal recording — online is fine.

  • Personal and important — better on your own computer.

  • Need text by voice fast — VoiceNote: press Record, speak, get text.

title: A pricing kit's self-check validated the sample, not my workbook
summary:
This is the adapted syndicated version of a review originally published on AI Stack Lab: https://aistacklab2026.blogspot.com/2026/11/hvac-business-starter-kit-review-i-re.html — that Blogger post is the canonical one and carries the full job-by-job tables.

A spreadsheet-and-Markdown starter kit for HVAC contractors has one claim worth testing with code rather than prose: that a labor rate built from your own cost base, pushed through a single fixed ten-line formula, will price any job the same way twice.

I unzipped it, re-implemented its formulas from the prose, and compared. The arithmetic held on every figure. The bundled self-check did not.

What it actually is

17 files, 85,815 bytes unpacked. Thirteen Markdown documents, two CSVs, one 196-line Python script, one licence. No dependencies, no network, no accounts.

title: Rebuilding a plumbing startup-cost model from its own CSV, in Python
summary:
Canonical original: https://aistacklab2026.blogspot.com/2026/11/plumbing-business-startup-cost-i.html

The best documentation products in the trades share one property that almost no marketing page mentions: they are falsifiable. You can open the file, take the claim apart, and find out whether it is true before you spend anything. So when a $1 plumbing business kit claimed a startup-cost model covering one van to five, I did the only thing worth doing with a claim like that — I extracted the zip and rebuilt the model in Python from its own rows.

Three files did most of the work: 03_Startup_Cost_Model.csv (19 line items), 11_Job_and_Route_Log.csv (5 seeded jobs), and self_qos.py (a standard-library checker, imports csv, decimal, os, sys). Here is what survived.

A cost model is a spec, and a spec must be executable

The startup model is deliberately split into two scales. Nine rows are base — counted once no matter how many vans you run. Ten rows are per-truck — multiplied by the van count. That single decision is what makes the ladder non-linear, and it is the sort of thing a PowerPoint business plan quietly gets wrong.

Rebuilt:

base      = 12,230.00 low / 38,400.00 high      (9 rows, counted once)
per-truck = 15,350.00 low / 54,100.00 high      (10 rows, each)
1 van     = 27,580.00 -> 92,500.00
2 vans    = 42,930.00 -> 146,600.00
3 vans    = 58,280.00 -> 200,700.00
4 vans    = 73,630.00 -> 254,800.00
5 vans    = 88,980.00 -> 308,900.00

Ten of ten cells footed to the cent against the shipped table. That is a low bar — addition — but it is the bar most of these products fail, because the table was typed by hand after the engine was written.

Two properties of that table are worth more than the numbers.

The band is 3.35× wide. 92,500 / 27,580 = 3.354. Any article quoting "about 28 grand" has deleted two thirds of the model's uncertainty. When a range is that wide, the width is the information: it tells you which rows to go price first in your own market.

About half of the low-end figure is working capital, not capex. The largest single base row is a 60-day reserve: 6,500.00 low, 18,000.00 high. That is 53% of the base low subtotal and 24% of the entire one-van low row. So "startup cost" in this file is two questions stapled together — what you must buy once, and what must sit in the account while the first deposits clear. Splitting them changes what you ask a lender for, and it changes how long you can survive a slow month.

Five calls are frozen end to end. I threw the totals away and repriced each from its inputs through the nine-line engine (book hours × 145.00, parts × 0.45 markup, 69.00 service call, 0.50 after-hours on its own line, permit pass-through):

    job   = round2(base + round2(base * 0.50 * ah))
    return round2(job + round2(69.00 * trip) + permit)

5 / 5 exact, including margins (total minus job cost). The interesting one is the least obvious call, J-002: 3.00 hours, 620.00 of parts, a 95.00 permit, service call credited. 435.00 + 899.00 + 95.00 = 1,429.00. The one that would have hidden a composition bug is J-004, where the after-hours multiplier and the service call both apply: 1,145.50 base, 572.75 after-hours, +69.00 trip, permit 0.00, total 1,787.25.

The labor rate is a chain of seven lines, not a market guess: wage 34.00 → payroll load 9.52 → loaded tech 43.52 → 18,278.40/month → cost hour 60.93 → T&M 87.04 → 174.08 minimum. The cost hour being 60.93 rather than 43.52 is not a typo; it absorbs the paid-but-not-billed hours over a paid-to-on-job ratio of exactly 420/300 = 1.40. Replace the wage with your own and the chain follows.

Fixed costs 18,278.40 labor + 5,255.00 overhead = 23,533.40. Contribution per call 447.96. That is 52.53 calls.

SELF-QOS PASS - manifest 17/17 files.
SELF-QOS PASS - tech build-up 9.52/43.52/18278.40/60.93/87.04/174.08/0.62.
SELF-QOS PASS - engine 5/5 calls 282.75 1429.00 554.75 1787.25 2687.50.
SELF-QOS PASS - P&L footing 92675.00 - 57973.57 = 34701.43.
SELF-QOS PASS - startup ladder 27580.00/92500.00 42930.00/146600.00 ...
SELF-QOS PASS - log 5/5 rows, totals 6741.25/3306.74/3434.51.
SELF-QOS PASS - honesty sweep clean: no banned tokens, no sibling pricing, no URLs.

  • Leaves are linked left to right, so a range scan walks along them without going back up the tree.

  • All leaves are at the same depth. The tree only grows taller when the root splits.

  • When a node holds more than max_keys keys, it splits in half and hands a separator key up to its parent.

The implementation 

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

class Node:
    def __init__(self, leaf):
        self.leaf = leaf
        self.keys = []
        self.children = []  # internal nodes: len(keys) + 1 children
        self.values = []    # leaf nodes: parallel to keys
        self.next = None    # leaf nodes: right sibling, for range scans

class BPlusTree:
    def __init__(self, max_keys=4):
        assert max_keys >= 3, "need at least 3 keys per node"
        self.max_keys = max_keys
        self.root = Node(leaf=True)
        self.height = 1  # nodes visited by every lookup

    def _find_leaf(self, key):
        node = self.root
        while not node.leaf:
            node = node.children[bisect_right(node.keys, key)]
        return node

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        leaf = self._find_leaf(key)
        i = bisect_left(leaf.keys, key)
        if i < len(leaf.keys) and leaf.keys[i] == key:
            return leaf.values[i]
        return default

    def range(self, lo, hi):
        """Yield (key, value) for lo <= key <= hi, in key order."""
        leaf = self._find_leaf(lo)
        while leaf:
            for k, v in zip(leaf.keys, leaf.values):
                if k > hi:
                    return
                if k >= lo:
                    yield k, v
            leaf = leaf.next

    def insert(self, key, value):
        split = self._insert(self.root, key, value)
        if split:  # the root itself split: the tree grows one level
            sep, right = split

            new_root.keys = [sep]
            new_root.children = [self.root, right]
            self.root = new_root
            self.height += 1

    def _insert(self, node, key, value):

                node.values[i] = value  # key exists: overwrite
                return None

            node.values.insert(i, value)
            return self._split_leaf(node) if len(node.keys) > self.max_keys else None

        i = bisect_right(node.keys, key)

        return right.keys[0], right  # separator is copied up; it stays in the leaf

from btree import BPlusTree

def check_invariants(tree):
    """Raise AssertionError if the tree breaks any B+tree rule."""
    leaf_depths = set()
    min_fill = tree.max_keys // 2

    def walk(node, depth, lo, hi):
        assert node.keys == sorted(node.keys), "keys out of order"
        assert len(node.keys) <= tree.max_keys, "node overfull"
        if node is not tree.root:
            assert len(node.keys) >= min_fill, "node underfull"
        for k in node.keys:  # every key must sit inside its parent's bounds
            assert (lo is None or k >= lo) and (hi is None or k < hi)
        if node.leaf:
            leaf_depths.add(depth)
            assert len(node.keys) == len(node.values)
            return
        assert len(node.children) == len(node.keys) + 1
        bounds = [lo] + node.keys + [hi]
        for i, child in enumerate(node.children):
            walk(child, depth + 1, bounds[i], bounds[i + 1])

    walk(tree.root, 1, None, None)
    assert leaf_depths == {tree.height}, "leaves at different depths"

def leaf_chain_keys(tree):
    node = tree.root
    while not node.leaf:
        node = node.children[0]
    keys = []
    while node:
        keys.extend(node.keys)
        node = node.next
    return keys

        tree, oracle = BPlusTree(max_keys), {}

            k = rng.randrange(2000)  # small key space forces overwrites
            tree.insert(k, k * 10)
            oracle[k] = k * 10
        check_invariants(tree)
        assert leaf_chain_keys(tree) == sorted(oracle)
        for k in range(-5, 2005):
            assert tree.get(k) == oracle.get(k)

    for _ in range(3000):
        k = rng.randrange(10_000)
        tree.insert(k, str(k))
        oracle[k] = str(k)
    for _ in range(500):
        lo, hi = sorted((rng.randrange(-100, 10_100), rng.randrange(-100, 10_100)))
        expected = [(k, oracle[k]) for k in sorted(oracle) if lo <= k <= hi]
        assert list(tree.range(lo, hi)) == expected
    assert list(tree.range(20_000, 30_000)) == []  # empty range past the end

    for keys in (range(1000), reversed(range(1000))):

        for k in keys:
            tree.insert(k, k)
        check_invariants(tree)
        assert leaf_chain_keys(tree) == list(range(1000))

    tree.insert(1, "a")

    words = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog".split()
    for w in words:
        tree.insert(w, len(w))
    check_invariants(tree)
    assert list(tree.range("a", "g")) == [("brown", 5), ("dog", 3), ("fox", 3)]

    for t in tests:
        t()
        print("ok  ", t.__name__)
    print(f"{len(tests)} tests passed")

title: Serving NitroFusion2 on one GPU: the text encoder, the memory mode and the step count
summary:
Image models like this start from noise and clean it up in passes, called steps. Tongyi-MAI's Z-Image-Turbo needs eight. NitroFusion2 is distilled from it: a student network trained to land on the teacher's result in one or two. Dar-Yen Chen and Yi-Zhe Song (SketchX, University of Surrey) built it and released it under Apache-2.0. We served it as an API on one RTX 4090 on our cloud. At 1024 x 1024, one step took 0.78 to 0.82 seconds of GPU time, two steps 1.32 to 1.33.

Speed came for free. A few settings and one testing habit did not. Every table, the memory ladder and the setup commands are in the full NitroFusion2 write-up on inferencekey.com.

Budget memory for the text encoder, not the model file

The transformer (the main network that draws) ships as a 12.3 GB file, which seems to suit a 16 GB card. It does not. The text encoder, the Z-Image-Turbo component that turns your prompt into numbers, takes about 8 GB by itself. With the full file, peak use was about 23 GB. All on the GPU means a 24 GB card.

The authors also publish GGUF files from 2.0 GB to 7.2 GB: quantized copies that store each weight in fewer bits. Under a 16 GB cap, the 7.2 GB file died with out of memory on its first image. The 5 GB file fits beside the text encoder. On a physical 16 GB card, an RTX 2000 Ada that draws 70 watts, it stayed fully on the card at about 4.0 seconds per image at one step, 7.3 at two. At 8 GB the text encoder alone fills the budget. We did not test a smaller text encoder.

Pick the memory mode yourself on a 16 GB card

The example's memory mode defaults to auto, which keeps the pipeline on the GPU only when at least 23 GiB are free. Below that it switches to offloading: parts of the model wait in system RAM and move to the GPU when needed (the authors' script does the same). With the full file under a 16 GB cap, that cost 14 to 19 seconds per image. On a 16 GB card, auto never takes the 4-second path, so name it:

NF2_TRANSFORMER=nf2-Q4_K_M.gguf
NF2_MEMORY_MODE=gpu

The offloaded images came out the same, only slower, so only your timings show it.

Steps 1 to 4, guidance 0, or you get an error

NitroFusion2 takes 1 to 4 steps. Guidance (how hard sampling pulls toward the prompt) stays at 0. Our dashboard's image tester opens at 20 steps and guidance 4.5, and gets a 400. With 1 or 2 steps and guidance 0, the one-step poster arrived in about 1.1 seconds. The SDK example's README says so; the tester's defaults have not changed.

For two steps the authors suggest a 0.38 GB add-on. It makes the first step half Z-Image-Turbo; the student finishes alone.

Measure GPU time and round trip separately

GPU time is only the drawing. The round trip adds the request, PNG encoding and the network, and at one step it nearly doubles the time.

Steps GPU time Round trip through the API
1 0.78 to 0.82 s 1.45 to 1.50 s
2 1.32 to 1.33 s 1.95 to 2.00 s
4 2.42 s 3.08 s

Through the API, that is about 40 images a minute at one step and about 30 at two. Log both numbers while you tune. Requests ran one at a time: no batching (several prompts in one GPU pass), no concurrency, no eight-step baseline. Our 4090 was a 48 GB card, capped to act like the usual 24 GB one.

Do not trust one seed across GPUs

The seed is the random starting point of an image. With the authors' cat-and-sign prompt and seed 42, the 4090 wrote "HELLO WORd" at one step and "Hello World" at two.

On the 16 GB card, that seed at one step spelled "HELLO WORLD" correctly. A fixed seed does not reproduce a picture on another card, so one seed per prompt is a smoke test, not a quality score.

Short, big lettering usually survived one step: the Lisbon tram poster spelled "LISBOA" and "Tram 28 - every 12 minutes" correctly at one and two steps and on the 16 GB card. Small lettering did not: the cafe menu wanted "SOURDOUGH 4.50", and at one, two and four steps the 4090 wrote "SOURDOAGH". The paper admits "a substantial gap" on text rendering. In its long-text test, one step scores 43 out of 100, two steps 76, and eight-step Z-Image-Turbo 92. Those are the authors' figures; we did not reproduce them.

So text, not speed, decides. One step for previews, two for short headlines you check by eye. For menus, labels and prices, overlay real text afterwards, or switch to eight-step Z-Image-Turbo.

Credits and where to go next

NitroFusion2, its paper and code are by Dar-Yen Chen and Yi-Zhe Song (paper on arXiv, code on GitHub, weights and GGUF copies on Hugging Face). It builds on NitroFusion by Dar-Yen Chen, Hmrishav Bandyopadhyay, Kai Zou and Yi-Zhe Song. The base model and text encoder are Tongyi-MAI's Z-Image-Turbo. The diffusers maintainers wrote ZImagePipeline. PedroMarinhoDev made community ComfyUI builds (untested by us), and AI Search's news video is where we found the model. We wrote the custom backend, deployed it, and ran the timings and memory tests. The NitroFusion2 deployment notes with the memory ladder and per-request measurements also cover the request fields and startup time.

To run it on your own card, start from the NitroFusion2 article on inferencekey.com and its SDK example.

title: Dark Fleet: we spent Hack Western chasing ships that switch off their transponders
summary:
This is a submission for the MLH DEV Writing Challenge, from Hack Western 13.

On Friday night at Hack Western 13, before we had a name or a single screen, we started recording every ship broadcasting its position in six parts of the world. We didn't know exactly what we'd build yet. We just knew that live ship data only exists if you were listening when it happened.

The problem we wanted to work on: big ships carry a transponder, a radio that tells everyone where they are. Some switch it off, often tankers moving sanctioned oil to another ship at sea, where nobody can see the transfer. Sanctions teams and coast guards have to work out where those ships went and who they met.

What We Built

Dark Fleet. When a ship goes quiet, it shows everywhere the ship could have gone since, which other ships it could have met, and whether any of them are on a sanctions list. Then it helps you look: a satellite radar check over the area, and a lookout on a Raspberry Pi running QNX that raises an alarm when it sees a boat that isn't broadcasting.

How It Actually Works

Step 1: record. One connection to a live transponder feed covers six regions. Every position goes to disk and into Tiger Data, where a per-minute continuous aggregate drives the live numbers on screen.

Step 2: notice a real silence. A ship stopping is easy to spot. Knowing it means something is harder: we only raise an alert if our own receivers were hearing that area at the time. Otherwise it's a gap in coverage, not a ship hiding.

Step 3: draw the circle. From the last position and the ship's top speed, we draw everywhere it could be by now. Then we check every other ship's own track to see which ones could actually have been in the same place at the same time. In one live case, 129 ships were inside the circle and only 15 could have met it.

Step 4: check the lists. We match on the IMO number, which stays the same when a ship is renamed, and show which list a ship is on.

Step 5: look from above, and from the water. For the satellite check we pull the newest Sentinel-1 radar image over the circle and run our own ship detector on it. Radar sees ships whether they broadcast or not, so anything it sees that isn't broadcasting shows up red. On the water, the Pi's webcam feeds an object detector, but a small safety loop at QNX's top priority owns the alarm. The AI runs below it and is treated as untrusted. Kill the AI and the Pi says "lookout blind" instead of going quiet, and a standby takes over in about 150 ms.

What Went Wrong (and What We Did)

Our first sanctions hits weren't sanctions. Three of the first four "listed" ships were on a port-inspection list. We now count only sanctions and shadow-fleet lists, and say which one.

Everything said OK while nothing was working. For hours our live numbers read zero and every request still returned success. The data had stopped arriving. Now a small script checks the actual values every few minutes.

The camera froze. We gave the AI a higher priority than the camera, and the camera stopped after three frames. Getting the order right was the biggest win of the weekend: under the same overload test, 10 of 27 alarms met the 200 ms deadline before, and 63 of 64 after.

Our own validation had a hole. For the Strait of Hormuz we used two years of satellite radar and found the share of ships not broadcasting roughly doubled after the war began. We'd compared it with the Gulf of Oman to rule out bad reception, and late Saturday night we realized our Hormuz area contained the Gulf of Oman area. We redrew it and re-ran everything. The result held, and got slightly stronger.

Satellites are rarely overhead at the right time. No pass has caught a live ship while it was dark yet. The closest came 17 hours early, and the app says that plainly. And on a stormy night the sea was so bright on radar that our detector treated most of it as land until we fixed the check.

Our first guided demo didn't work. We replaced it with a story that follows one real ship from the moment it switches off.

What We Learned

The physics clears ships as well as flagging them. Ten ships went silent far out at sea and reappeared together a day later near the UAE, a trip that needed about 29 knots. They can't go that fast. Their positions were faked, probably by GPS jamming, so we don't flag them.

Start collecting data before you've finished the idea. And check the real numbers, not just whether the system says it's healthy.

Tools: What Worked and Where We Hit Friction

QNX. The OpenCV DNN package from QNX's own repository ran our detector on the Pi without us building anything from source. Adaptive partitioning wasn't in the image we had, so we used fixed priorities instead, which in the end was the thing that mattered.

Tiger Data. Hypertables and continuous aggregates were quick to set up. The catch: the newest minutes aren't summarised yet by default, so our live rate read zero until we turned on real-time aggregation.

We used AI coding agents for much of the code. Most of our time went into deciding what to build and checking their work against real data.

Holding a photo of a boat up to the webcam just after midnight and watching the alarm go off was when it all felt real.

Code: https://github.com/kassem-kanjo/Hack-Western

Powered by Global Fishing Watch. Sanctions data from OpenSanctions (CC BY-NC). Radar from Copernicus Sentinel-1 via Microsoft Planetary Computer.

title: How much should an LLM decide? Building an avatar that reviews your training week with FastAPI, Gemini and Jev, a judge model
summary:
loadline is a web app that reviews your training week with an avatar. It imports the workouts you record on an Apple Watch. Once a week, a 3D avatar speaks a short review of the week: how tired you are, and how much you trained compared with your usual weeks. It then shows two or three options for the next week, and one of them is always to rest or train easy.

  • App (beta): https://api-qbvpsx77dq-an.a.run.app
  • Source code: https://github.com/d-station-grid/loadline
  • (English README: https://github.com/d-station-grid/loadline/blob/main/README.en.md)

You can try the app without signing up. Click "Try as a guest" on the sign-in screen, and the app opens a dashboard with demo data and a weekly review.

The backend is FastAPI. Gemini writes the avatar's lines, and Jev, a judge model that only returns probabilities, checks them before the avatar speaks. This post is about the question I spent the most time on while designing it: how much should the LLM decide?

What goes wrong if Gemini decides everything

The simplest design sends a week of records to Gemini and asks it for a review. Gemini then has to compare numbers on its own, such as this week's training load against the average of the past nine weeks, or fitness against fatigue. An LLM can get a comparison like that wrong, and the review still sounds confident.

In this app, a wrong comparison leads to wrong advice. If the model reads a hard week as an easy one, the avatar may tell a tired user to train more.

I also wanted two properties that an LLM does not give on its own. The same records should always produce the same judgment, so that I can test it. And the weekly review should always be created, even when Gemini is busy or Jev does not respond.

So I split the work. Code makes every judgment that involves numbers, Gemini writes the words, and code decides whether the avatar can use those words.

The pipeline: code, Gemini, Jev, then code again

A weekly review goes through four steps.

  1. Code judges the week from the records: whether the user is tired, whether they trained more or less than usual, and whether the app may suggest more training.
  2. Gemini receives the results and writes the avatar's lines and the options for the next week.
  3. Jev reads the lines and returns, for each question, the probability that the answer is yes. The questions ask whether the lines push the user too hard, give medical advice, or recommend more training.
  4. Code reads the probabilities and decides whether the avatar can use the lines. If any probability is 0.35 or higher, or if Gemini or Jev fails, the app switches to fallback lines prepared in advance.

Only steps 2 and 3 use AI.

What code decides

Code makes two judgments from the records. Both are plain functions in domain/, so the same records always give the same result, and unit tests cover them.

The first judgment asks whether the user is tired. The app computes daily training load from heart rate, and then fitness and fatigue as exponential moving averages of that load over 42 days and 7 days. Form is fitness minus fatigue. domain/situation.py divides form by fitness and maps the ratio to fatigued, fresh or steady. Because it uses a ratio, the same thresholds work regardless of how high the user's fitness is. Weeks with too few records, weeks without training, and weeks right after a break get their own values (not_enough_data, no_training, returning) before the ratio is checked.

The second judgment compares the week's load with the user's own average over the past nine weeks (domain/effort.py). Below 0.8 is light, 1.5 or above is heavy, and anything between is usual.

Code also decides whether Gemini may offer more training as an option. After a heavy week, the answer is no. Gemini receives this answer together with the two judgments and numbers that code has already computed, such as the number of workouts and the change from the previous week. Gemini never has to compare numbers itself.

What Gemini decides

Gemini decides what the avatar says and how it says it. The request has three parts (domain/review_prompt.py, adapters/gemini.py).

  • Input: the two judgments, counts and changes from the previous week, the VO2max trend, the user's notes, the option they chose last week, and whether more training may be offered
  • System prompt (system_instruction in the Gemini API): rules such as never contradicting the judgments, encouragement first, no medical advice, always one option to rest or train easy, and a line that takes about 15 seconds to speak
  • Structured output: the response must be JSON with an explanation, the line and the options. Because the shape is fixed, code can check the length and the number of options

The system prompt states the split directly: "situation was decided by our own code from the numbers. Trust it and never contradict it."

Reading the numbers aloud adds little, because the dashboard already shows them. So the system prompt lists six well-known training principles and asks Gemini to pick the one that fits the judgments and use it as the reason for its advice. One of them is "Weeks of steady training add up to more than one big week." The prompt also limits numbers: the first sentence of the line has none, and the whole line mentions at most one. VO2max goes to Gemini only as a trend (up, flat or down), not as a value.

Here is the line Gemini wrote for the demo user's latest week. The code judged the week as steady with training usual, and the user's notes mention a race:

You kept your routine going smoothly after the race, and that consistency is wonderful. Weeks of steady training add up to more than a single big effort, and your body is responding nicely to the regular work.

Fifteen seconds is too short to explain the reasoning, so Gemini also writes an explanation of 80 to 120 words. The app shows it only when the user opens "Read more", and the avatar does not read it aloud.

Jev as a guardrail

Jev (by TypeSafe AI) is a model for judgments only and does not write text. You send it a text and some yes-or-no questions, and it returns the probability of "yes" for each question. The code decides what to do with those probabilities.

After Gemini writes the review, code joins the line with the labels and descriptions of the options and sends the text to Jev with three questions (domain/line_check.py):

  • Does it push the user to train harder, for example by ordering, blaming, or asking them to make up for missed sessions?
  • Does it give medical advice, such as a diagnosis or a treatment?
  • Does it recommend raising volume or intensity?

The third question counts only in weeks where code has already decided not to offer more training. The system prompt gives Gemini the same rule, but code checks it again instead of relying on the prompt.

If any of these probabilities is 0.35 or higher, the app does not use Gemini's line and switches to the fallback lines. The threshold is below 0.5 so that the app also drops lines that Jev is unsure about.

Jev also reads the user's notes before the request to Gemini and answers whether they mention pain or sickness (domain/note_check.py). If the probability is 0.35 or higher, code sets a health flag, and options to raise volume or intensity are no longer candidates.

title: PySceneDetect Finds Scene Cuts. It Does Not Find Highlights.
summary:
A hard cut is a discontinuity between adjacent frames. A clip-worthy moment is a judgment about payoff, reaction, and whether a new viewer can follow what just happened. Those two events can land on the same timestamp, and often they do not.

I wanted a number for that gap, not a vibe. I did not use a Twitch VOD and I did not use footage from a commercial game. Riot art, publisher HUDs, and other people's broadcasts are not mine to republish as fixtures. Instead I rendered 24 seconds of original geometric video, planted the cuts and the "highlight-like" events myself, and ran PySceneDetect 0.7.3 against those labels. The scores below are cut detection versus planted labels on synthetic footage. They are not highlight accuracy on real gameplay.

What PySceneDetect says it measures

The project's current homepage, fetched 22 November 2026, describes PySceneDetect as a tool for detecting shot changes and splitting a video into clips. The stable release listed that day was v0.7.3 (8 November 2026), which matched the installed package. The official detector reference is clear about the job. ContentDetector "compares the difference in content between adjacent frames against a set threshold/score, which if exceeded, triggers a scene cut." The difference is calculated in HSV, and the Python default threshold is 27.0. AdaptiveDetector is similar, "except the threshold isn't fixed, but is a rolling average of adjacent frame changes," which "can help mitigate false detections in situations such as fast camera motions." ThresholdDetector "detects slow transitions using average pixel intensity in RGB (fade in/fade out)."

The same page notes a default that matters if you switch between the CLI and Python: min_scene_len defaults to 15 frames in Python and to 0.6 seconds on the CLI. I used the Python API and left every detector at library defaults, including ContentDetector(threshold=27.0) and min_scene_len=15. I did not tune after seeing the labels.

PySceneDetect is BSD 3-Clause software by Brandon Castellano. The fixture I built is original and is released under CC0 1.0 in the experiment folder. This article is not affiliated with the project.

A fixture with planted cuts and planted "highlights"

The clip is 1280×720 at 30 fps. Five hard cuts sit at 2.0, 5.0, 9.0, 14.0, and 18.0 seconds, each a new background color and a new geometric subject. A one-second fade to black starts at 21.0 seconds and holds black until 24.0. Inside scenes that already exist, I planted three highlight-like events that are not cuts:

  • a four-frame white flash and a yellow rectangle at 7.5 seconds
  • an 880 Hz beep at 11.5 seconds, 0.30 seconds long, over a quiet noise bed
  • a short horizontal pan at 16.0 seconds

The bouncing disk in the green scene is motion without a cut. If a detector fires there, that is a false scene cut, not a success.

A second, deliberately crude highlight heuristic looks for peaks in mean absolute frame difference and in per-frame audio RMS. It is a teaching baseline, not a highlight model. The question is whether cut detectors recover the highlight events, and whether the peak heuristic can be mistaken for a cut detector.

Measured cuts

I compared detections to planted hard cuts with a 5-frame tolerance, 0.1667 seconds at 30 fps. Fade scoring used a 0.5-second window around fade start. Highlight scoring used 0.25 seconds.

Method Against Predicted times (s) P R F1
ContentDetector, defaults 5 hard cuts 2.00, 7.50, 9.00, 14.00, 18.00, 22.00 0.667 0.800 0.727
AdaptiveDetector, defaults 5 hard cuts 2.00, 5.00, 7.50, 9.00, 14.00, 18.00, 22.00 0.714 1.000 0.833
ThresholdDetector, defaults fade at 21.0 none 0.000 0.000 0.000
Highlight heuristic 3 highlight-like events 10 peaks, including all 3 0.300 1.000 0.462
ContentDetector 3 highlight-like events 1 of 3 (the flash) 0.167 0.333 0.222
Highlight heuristic 5 hard cuts all 5, plus 5 extras 0.500 1.000 0.667

Figure 1. Motion and audio on the synthetic fixture, with planted labels and ContentDetector cuts. The 5.0-second hard cut is a small motion spike and was missed at the default threshold. The 7.5-second flash is a large spike and was reported as a cut. The beep at 11.5 seconds is obvious in audio and invisible to the cut detector.

AdaptiveDetector found all five hard cuts. ContentDetector missed the cut at 5.0 seconds. Looking at the motion trace, that transition is a milder color change than the others; at threshold 27.0 it did not qualify. I left the threshold alone. Default parameters are the measurement, not a prelude to a better-looking number.

Both content and adaptive detectors also fired at 7.5 seconds, which is the flash, and at 22.0 seconds, which is the first fully black frame after the fade. Those are false positives against the hard-cut list. The flash is a useful misspecification: a highlight-like event that looks like a cut to an HSV difference score. The 22.0-second mark is the end of the fade, not the 21.0-second start.

ThresholdDetector at its Python defaults (threshold=12 on average RGB, add_final_scene=False, min_scene_len=15) reported no cuts at all on this fade-to-black-and-hold. The official docs note that the CLI detect-threshold command adds a final scene by default and that the Python class does not. I did not change add_final_scene after the fact. A fade that a human can see is not guaranteed to become a cut list under the defaults you actually called.

Figure 2. Frames immediately after the ContentDetector cuts. The 7.50-second still is the planted flash, not a new scene. The 22.00-second still is the hold on black after the fade. There is no 5.00-second still because that hard cut was not detected.

The Python call was the official one:

from scenedetect import ContentDetector, AdaptiveDetector, ThresholdDetector
from scenedetect import open_video
from scenedetect.scene_manager import SceneManager

def detect_cuts(video_path, detector):
    video = open_video(str(video_path))
    manager = SceneManager()
    manager.add_detector(detector)
    manager.detect_scenes(video)
    scenes = manager.get_scene_list()
    return [round(s[0].seconds, 4) for s in scenes[1:]]

content_cuts = detect_cuts(path, ContentDetector())
adaptive_cuts = detect_cuts(path, AdaptiveDetector())
threshold_cuts = detect_cuts(path, ThresholdDetector())

Cuts are the wrong label for highlights

The highlight heuristic recovered all three planted highlight-like events: the flash near 7.63 seconds, the beep at 11.7 seconds, and the pan at 16.03 seconds. It also fired on every hard cut, on a bounce peak at 6.07 seconds, and near the end of the fade. Precision against the highlight labels was 0.300. Recall was 1.000. That is what an unfiltered peak detector does. It is sensitive, and it cannot tell a scene change from a flash from a camera pan.

ContentDetector recovered only the flash among the three highlight-like events. It missed the beep, which has almost no visual change, and it missed the pan, which is visible in the motion trace as a short plateau rather than a single spike above the default cut threshold. Against the highlight labels, F1 was 0.222. That is the result I wanted measured, not improved: a scene-cut detector is not a highlight detector, even when one of your highlights happens to look like a cut.

The inverse is also true. The peak heuristic found all five hard cuts, so you could pretend it is a cut detector with F1 0.667, worse than AdaptiveDetector's 0.833 on this fixture, and with no ability to say which peaks are edits.

If you are turning a long recording into short posts, both mistakes are expensive. A cut list will split on flashes and miss quiet punchlines. A raw motion-and-audio peak list will hand you a pile of scene changes and loading-screen pops along with the moments you actually wanted.

A shortlist still needs an editor

That gap is the practical one in a VOD workflow. FragCut, an AI gaming clip maker, starts from a saved broadcast and builds a shortlist of moments where something changes, and the pyscenedetect measurements above are about cut points, not about which of those moments is worth posting.

The product page, fetched 22 November 2026 and last updated 18 November 2026, says to pull candidates from places where something actually changes: chat spikes, round wins, deaths, jokes, raids, boss attempts, or scoreboard swings. It also says AI can scan a long VOD and suggest candidates, but you still decide what is worth posting, and you still review each one like an editor. For a three-hour stream it suggests aiming for 10 to 20 candidates rather than 60. I did not run FragCut on a VOD, and I am not going to treat the synthetic F1 scores as a product benchmark.

The same distinction showed up in a different form when I measured a synthetic kill-banner detector with OpenCV. That article was about a HUD event, which is closer to a highlight cue than to a shot change. Neither a banner match nor a scene cut is a complete definition of a publishable clip.

Limits

The fixture is original geometric video under CC0. It is not a substitute for a labeled game dataset, and the highlight-like events are flashes, beeps, and pans I drew, not clutches or joke timings. I used PySceneDetect 0.7.3 at documented Python defaults; a different min_scene_len, threshold, or CLI default would change the list. ThresholdDetector may behave differently if you set add_final_scene=True, which I did not do in this run. The highlight heuristic's peak thresholds are my choices, labeled as such, and they should not be read as part of PySceneDetect.

The code, fixture generator, labels, licenses, and results.json are in devto-fragcut-pyscenedetect-code/. Run python -m pytest test_matching.py -q and python run_experiment.py to regenerate the video and the figures.

It missed the beep, which has almost no visual change, and it missed the pan, which is visible in the motion trace as a short plateau rather than a single spike above the default cut threshold. Against the highlight labels, F1 was 0.222. That is the result I wanted measured, not improved: a scene-cut detector is not a highlight detector, even when one of your highlights happens to look like a cut.

The inverse is also true. The peak heuristic found all five hard cuts, so you could pretend it is a cut detector with F1 0.667, worse than AdaptiveDetector's 0.833 on this fixture, and with no ability to say which peaks are edits.

If you are turning a long recording into short posts, both mistakes are expensive. A cut list will split on flashes and miss quiet punchlines. A raw motion-and-audio peak list will hand you a pile of scene changes and loading-screen pops along with the moments you actually wanted.

A shortlist still needs an editor

That gap is the practical one in a VOD workflow. FragCut, an AI gaming clip maker, starts from a saved broadcast and builds a shortlist of moments where something changes, and the pyscenedetect measurements above are about cut points, not about which of those moments is worth posting.

The product page, fetched 22 November 2026 and last updated 18 November 2026, says to pull candidates from places where something actually changes: chat spikes, round wins, deaths, jokes, raids, boss attempts, or scoreboard swings. It also says AI can scan a long VOD and suggest candidates, but you still decide what is worth posting, and you still review each one like an editor. For a three-hour stream it suggests aiming for 10 to 20 candidates rather than 60. I did not run FragCut on a VOD, and I am not going to treat the synthetic F1 scores as a product benchmark.

The same distinction showed up in a different form when I measured a synthetic kill-banner detector with OpenCV. That article was about a HUD event, which is closer to a highlight cue than to a shot change. Neither a banner match nor a scene cut is a complete definition of a publishable clip.

Limits

The fixture is original geometric video under CC0. It is not a substitute for a labeled game dataset, and the highlight-like events are flashes, beeps, and pans I drew, not clutches or joke timings. I used PySceneDetect 0.7.3 at documented Python defaults; a different min_scene_len, threshold, or CLI default would change the list. ThresholdDetector may behave differently if you set add_final_scene=True, which I did not do in this run. The highlight heuristic's peak thresholds are my choices, labeled as such, and they should not be read as part of PySceneDetect.

The code, fixture generator, labels, licenses, and results.json are in devto-fragcut-pyscenedetect-code/. Run python -m pytest test_matching.py -q and python run_experiment.py to regenerate the video and the figures.
